subjects.label: Émigré counter-revolution: organization, foreign dependence and failed army
subjects.meaning: The princes and émigrés attempted propaganda, diplomacy and armed restoration, linking Artois and Calonne’s Turin court to Catholic resistance at Jalès and the failed Lyons conspiracy before relocating to Koblenz. Successive emigrant waves, noble and clerical grievances, Varennes and officer departures shaped the movement. Sincere loyalty and personal sacrifice coexisted with rank rivalry, weak finance and supply, unrealistic promises of foreign help and dependence on foreign strategy. Retreat after Valmy dispersed the principal émigré army; Condé’s surviving corps was an exception.
subjects.stance: Do not treat émigrés as a homogeneous force or the agents of western peasant revolt. Their political claims exceeded resources and dependable foreign commitment; Condé’s survival was an exception to wider military collapse.

subjects.label: Religion as the popular foundation of counter-revolution
subjects.meaning: The Civil Constitution and clerical oath made revolutionary policy a test of local religious loyalty. Conservative and patriotic newspapers polarized around ecclesiastical policy, while religious conflicts stimulated patriotic clubs. Schism and papal condemnation gave counter-revolution a popular moral cause beyond court and émigré interests. Lay pressure and persecution helped turn suspected priests into opponents; renewed toleration in1795 weakened a persistent grievance sustaining western insurgency.
subjects.stance: Religion gave resistance popular legitimacy that aristocratic restoration alone lacked. This does not imply every religious opponent shared a Bourbon programme or that local communities merely followed clerical instructions.

subjects.label: Constitution of 1791: executive limits and the completed settlement
subjects.meaning: Constitution-making separated powers and weakened the executive through limits on royal initiative and a suspensive veto, ministers outside the legislature and a three-year bar on deputies entering government; courts lost administrative authority. Property-based citizenship limited participation. After Varennes, conservatives completed the settlement, separated the Civil Constitution of the Clergy from the constitutional oath, restricted press freedom and altered suffrage: the silver-mark deputy test disappeared while secondary-elector qualifications rose after elections were already held. Amnesty and repeal of emigrant penalties did not halt officer departures. The king’s acceptance and public celebrations left religious, royal and republican divisions unresolved, although major administrative and legal institutions endured.
subjects.stance: Distinguish constitutional design, its enduring institutional effects and its failure to secure stable political legitimacy. The post-Varennes revisions neither recreated the earlier monarchien programme nor erased religious division or the king’s rejection of revolutionary terms. Lowering one qualification while raising another must not be reduced to a general expansion or contraction of suffrage.

subjects.label: National Guard: citizenship, political power and coercive social control
subjects.meaning: Citizens’ militias became the National Guard under Lafayette, with the Paris cockade later combined with Bourbon white as the tricolour. The Assembly relied on this popular force while seeking to contain crowds: municipal martial law authorized Guard fire on defiant demonstrators, and uniform costs, active-citizen rules, oaths and federations narrowed and disciplined membership. Distrust of the regular army and weak local enforcement made the Guard indispensable but unreliable. Units differed politically and confessionally: they could defend or constrain royal authority, embody Catholic or Protestant alignment, join rural disorder or repress the Champ de Mars petitioners.
subjects.stance: Do not equate the citizen army with a socially undifferentiated people or assume one stable political allegiance. Preserve local organization and the shifting coercive role.

After Varennes, conservatives completed the settlement, separated the Civil Constitution of the Clergy from the constitutional oath, restricted press freedom and altered suffrage: the silver-mark deputy test disappeared while secondary-elector qualifications rose after elections were already held. Amnesty and repeal of emigrant penalties did not halt officer departures. The king’s acceptance and public celebrations left religious, royal and republican divisions unresolved, although major administrative and legal institutions endured.

field_diffs.before: Legal design and political legitimacy must be distinguished. Final acceptance did not erase the incompatibility between revolutionary sovereignty and the king’s rejection of its terms.
field_diffs.after: Distinguish constitutional design, its enduring institutional effects and its failure to secure stable political legitimacy. The post-Varennes revisions neither recreated the earlier monarchien programme nor erased religious division or the king’s rejection of revolutionary terms. Lowering one qualification while raising another must not be reduced to a general expansion or contraction of suffrage.
